intro: For thirteen days in the summer of 1744 the brick courthouse of Lancaster, a German and Scots-Irish market town some sixty miles west of Philadelphia, held the largest Indian council the English colonies had yet staged. Deputies of the Haudenosaunee (Six Nations, "Iroquois") Confederacy, led by the Onöñda'gega' (Onondaga) speaker Canasatego, met Governor George Thomas of Pennsylvania and commissioners from Virginia and Maryland. The two southern colonies wanted the Confederacy's claims to land inside their charters extinguished; the Haudenosaunee wanted payment for lands already settled without purchase, an end to clashes with Virginians on the warriors' path south, and the alliance called the Covenant Chain kept bright. War between Britain and France had just been declared, and every party knew it. The background is the Philadelphia council of July 1742, where Canasatego complained that settlers from the south were living on unpurchased Haudenosaunee land west of the Susquehanna, and where he ordered the Lenape (Delaware) off the Forks of the Delaware in support of Pennsylvania's disputed Walking Purchase. A violent encounter between a Haudenosaunee war party and Virginia militia in the Shenandoah Valley that December made a settlement urgent; the interpreter Conrad Weiser carried Virginia's overtures to Onondaga in July 1743, with the botanist John Bartram in his company, and the meeting at Lancaster was the result. Almost all of the written record was made by the colonial side. The official minutes, printed by Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia in 1744 and attested by the Pennsylvania secretary Richard Peters, set down the Haudenosaunee speeches only as Conrad Weiser rendered them into English; no Haudenosaunee-authored text of the council survives, and the Confederacy's own record was kept in wampum and memory. Beside the minutes stand the private journal of Witham Marshe, secretary to the Maryland commissioners (first printed in 1801), Franklin's letters, Bartram's travel journal, Weiser's later journal of 1748, a Moravian account of Count Zinzendorf's 1742 covenant, and the Virginia commissioners' journal of the Logstown council of 1752. Several of these are letters, minutes and deeds rather than diaries, and are tagged as such. The heart of the chapter is the deed signed for Virginia on 2 July 1744. Virginia's commissioners asked for, and the chiefs signed, a release recognizing the King's right to all the lands within the colony; Virginia later read this as reaching to the Ohio under its sea-to-sea charter. Eight years later at Logstown a Haudenosaunee leader told Virginia's commissioners, as interpreted, that they had never understood the land sold to run west beyond the mountains. Both positions are set out here as the records give them. Two later afterlives of the council are also recorded. Canasatego's closing advice of 4 July, that the colonies should unite as the Five Nations had, was printed by Franklin and echoed in his 1751 letter on colonial union; whether and how far the Haudenosaunee example shaped later American federal thought is debated by historians and is presented here only as dated statements. And the exchange of 3–4 July over educating Haudenosaunee boys in Virginia, which the minutes record in a few lines, became in Franklin's 1784 retelling a celebrated story with a counter-offer that the minutes do not contain.

intro: On 20 August 1794, in a tangle of storm-felled trees beside the Maumee River, General Anthony Wayne's Legion broke the army of the western confederacy: Shaawanwaki (Shawnee), Lenape (Delaware), Wendat (Wyandot), Odawa (Ottawa), Anishinaabe (Ojibwe), Bodéwadmi (Potawatomi), Myaamia (Miami) and others, with Canadian volunteers. The retreat ran past Fort Miamis, a new British post on land the United States claimed. Later accounts, Indigenous and British, remembered its gates staying shut; the commandant's own letters record only a two-day argument with Wayne about whose soil the fort stood on. The defeat, and the plain evidence that Britain would not fight for its allies, sent leaders one by one to Wayne's headquarters at Fort Greenville over the winter. In January 1795 preliminary articles fixed a meeting for mid-June. From 16 June to early August, more than a thousand people from a dozen nations gathered there. Eleven languages were spoken; the record of what was said survives almost entirely in English. That is the central problem of this chapter. The fullest source is the official minutes kept by Wayne's secretary, Henry De Butts, and printed by Congress in 1832. Every Indigenous speech in them is an interpreter's English written down by the American side: Mihšihkinaahkwa (Little Turtle) through his son-in-law William Wells, Tarhe through Isaac Zane. Beside the minutes stand a surgeon's diary, a British spy's report, letters between Philadelphia and Greenville, and an anonymous soldier's journal of the 1794 campaign. There are few true diaries here, and the chapter is built mostly from minutes, letters and reports, labelled as such. The argument at Greenville was about which earlier paper counted. Wayne proposed the 1789 Treaty of Fort Harmar as the basis. Mihšihkinaahkwa said the Myaamia had never been party to it and set out their country by boundaries; Masass said the Ojibwe had been misinterpreted; Tarhe, who had signed it, defended its line as fair. Wayne answered with French forts, British treaties and conquest. The treaty signed on 3 August took most of present-day Ohio and declared the earlier treaties void, a point the Myaamia Center reads as a partial win for Mihšihkinaahkwa, though the line itself largely followed the old one. Some voices are missing. The Shawnee Tecumseh is said by his nineteenth-century biographers to have refused to attend, but no 1795 record of his refusal is known. The Moravian missionary David Zeisberger, then at Fairfield on the Thames in Upper Canada, kept a dated diary through these years (published 1885), but it could not be consulted for this chapter. Modern Myaamia scholarship, especially the Myaamia Center at Miami University, has reread the minutes from the Myaamia side and found other versions of Mihšihkinaahkwa's words; this chapter draws on that work.

intro: On 28 May 1830 Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act, which let the President offer lands west of the Mississippi in exchange for the homelands of nations in the East. Mississippi had already extended its state laws over the Chahta (Choctaw) Nation early that year. In mid-September the Secretary of War, John H. Eaton, and General John Coffee rode in carriages to a council ground on Chukfi Ahihla Bok, Dancing Rabbit Creek, in what is now Noxubee County. Several thousand Chahta people camped there, by district, under their three chiefs: Greenwood LeFlore, Mushulatubbee and Nitakechi. The council lasted about two weeks. The Chahta council voted down removal; many families went home believing the talks were over; the commissioners then negotiated with the leaders who remained. On 27 September a treaty was signed that ceded all Chahta land east of the Mississippi and set removal for the falls of 1831, 1832 and 1833. Its fourteenth article promised land in Mississippi to any head of a family who wished to stay and registered within six months. Supplementary articles of 28 September added reservations for named individuals. The honest record here is mostly letters, official papers and later testimony, not diaries. The commissioners kept a journal, now held in the National Archives (Record Group 75) and published with images by the Papers of Andrew Jackson; it could not be read directly for this chapter, so the council days are reconstructed from the treaty text, the commissioners' own letters as printed in 1830, newspaper correspondents, missionary letters, and the Chahta testimony collected by Henry S. Halbert and published in 1902, which the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma itself uses to tell the story. Chahta speeches survive only as interpreters' English (the United States interpreters were John Pitchlynn and M. Mackey) or as accounts told decades later. After the signing the record moves to the river. George S. Gaines took an exploring party west in October 1830 and superintended the first removal in 1831–32. Peter Pitchlynn, who opposed the treaty, led a party of about five hundred and kept a diary as he scouted the new country in January 1832. George W. Harkins wrote his farewell to the American people on a steamboat. Alexis de Tocqueville, waiting at Memphis in December 1831, watched a band of Chahta people cross the frozen-edged river and wrote to his mother about it on Christmas Day. The removals of 1831–33 moved some thirteen thousand people; the first winter was the hardest, and deaths along the route and in the first years in the West ran into the thousands by historians' estimates. Several thousand Chahta stayed in Mississippi, many of them failed by the fourteenth article's registration, whose shortfalls Congress was still investigating in 1837–38. Their descendants are today's Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians; the removed nation rebuilt in what is now Oklahoma.

intro: On 6 June 1835, beside a creek north of the Yarra River, John Batman handed blankets, knives, tomahawks and flour to a group of Kulin men and came away with two documents. They declared that eight ngurungaeta (headmen), three of them written down as 'Jagajaga', had granted about 600,000 acres around Port Phillip to him and his partners in return for those goods and a yearly 'rent or tribute'. It is the only documented attempt by colonists to make a treaty with Aboriginal people for their land in Australia. Within three months the Governor of New South Wales had declared it void. The record is lopsided, and this chapter says so plainly. Almost every word about the meeting comes from Batman himself: his journal, his deeds and his report to Governor Arthur. No Wurundjeri (Woiwurrung) or Boonwurrung (Bunurong) record from 1835 survives, and no one at the creek could translate between Woiwurrung and English; Batman's interpreters were Aboriginal men from the Sydney district who spoke another language. The ngurungaeta appear here as an eye made only of what the other side wrote down. William Barak, who said he watched as a boy, speaks only through memory recorded long afterward. What the elders understood is set out as positions, not settled. The deed reads as a grant of land. Historians such as Bain Attwood and Eva Bischoff, and Wurundjeri people today, point to tanderrum, the Kulin ceremony that welcomes visitors and gives them temporary access to Country in return for reciprocal obligations, as the likelier meaning of soil and gifts passing hand to hand. Gareth Knapman reads the deed's own legal form, drafted in Hobart by Joseph Gellibrand, as a feudal grant binding the grantees to a continuing tribute. William Buckley, the escaped convict who had lived with the Wadawurrung (Wathaurong) for thirty-two years, said in 1852 that no chief held a right over the soil that could be sold. Around the deed the record widens into letters and official papers: the camp journal of William Todd, left to hold the claim; the reports of the surveyor J. H. Wedge; the journal of John Pascoe Fawkner, whose rival party ignored the deed; Gellibrand's memoranda of a visit in 1836; and the despatches of Governors Arthur and Bourke and of Lord Glenelg in London. Bourke's proclamation of 26 August 1835 and Glenelg's approval of April 1836 settled the colonial law: the Crown alone could acquire land from Aboriginal people, and it treated the land as already its own. The epilogue is Melbourne. In March 1837 Bourke came to Port Phillip, approved the town plan and named the village on the Yarra; on 1 June 1837 the Crown sold the first town lots. The Association went on delivering tribute goods for a time, then stopped. The dates below let the purchaser, the people on the bank, the camp-keeper, the interpreter, the rival and the governors be read against one another, week by week.

intro: On 29 January 1840 HMS Herald brought Captain William Hobson into the Bay of Islands with orders to obtain British sovereignty over some or all of New Zealand with the free consent of its chiefs. Eight days later, on James Busby's lawn at Waitangi, more than forty rangatira of Ngāpuhi put their names or moko to a document written overnight in Māori by the missionary Henry Williams and his son. Through the autumn and winter of 1840 copies travelled the coasts by ship and on foot to about fifty meetings, and by September more than 500 rangatira, thirteen of them women, had signed, nearly all on the Māori text. Almost none of the record is diary in the strict sense. The Crown's side survives as Hobson's dispatches, Busby's draft and Williams's certified retranslation; the missionaries' as letters and, above all, William Colenso's notes of the 5 February debate, which he published only in 1890. The rangatira's own words survive in a narrower channel still: speeches given in Māori, rendered aloud into English by Williams, abridged on paper by Colenso and officials. Every speech in this chapter is labelled as interpreted for that reason. Two Americans, the consul James Clendon and the visiting commander Charles Wilkes, give outside views within weeks of the signing. The heart of the matter is that there were two texts. In the English, the chiefs ceded 'all the rights and powers of sovereignty' and were guaranteed 'exclusive and undisturbed possession' of their lands, forests and fisheries. In te Tiriti, the Māori text most rangatira heard and signed, they gave the Queen te kāwanatanga katoa, complete government, a word built on kāwana, governor, and the Queen confirmed to them te tino rangatiratanga, the full chiefly authority over their lands, homes and treasures. One reading holds that kāwanatanga conveyed sovereignty as the Crown intended; another holds that the rangatira agreed to share authority, keeping their own over their people. This chapter sets the texts and the spoken explanations side by side without choosing between them. On 14 November 2014 the Waitangi Tribunal released its stage 1 report on the Te Paparahi o Te Raki (Northland) inquiry, He Whakaputanga me te Tiriti, The Declaration and the Treaty. It concluded that the rangatira who signed in February 1840 did not cede sovereignty, that they agreed to share power with the Governor over British subjects, and that Britain intended to acquire sovereignty but did not explain this to them. The Tribunal stated that the report drew no conclusion about how the Crown later acquired the sovereignty it now exercises, or about what the treaty means today. Read together, the eyes show a negotiation conducted across a language gap by people with very different stakes: a governor needing a cession, missionaries vouching for him with their own credit, rangatira weighing a governor's protection against his power, a Catholic bishop securing a spoken promise, and foreign observers who already disagreed about what the signatures meant. Hobson proclaimed sovereignty on 21 May, before most of the sheets had come home.

intro: In September 1851 the largest gathering the northern Plains had seen camped along the North Platte: perhaps ten thousand people of the Oceti Sakowin (Sioux), Tsitsistas (Cheyenne), Hinono'eino (Arapaho), Apsáalooke (Crow), Nakoda (Assiniboine), Mandan, Hidatsa and Sahnish (Arikara), with a Newe (Shoshone) delegation that the commissioners would not admit to the treaty. Congress had voted $100,000 to buy safe passage for the overland roads. The grass at Fort Laramie gave out within days, so on 5 September the whole council moved thirty miles downriver to the mouth of Horse Creek, in what is now western Nebraska. The people there called it the Great Smoke. The record is almost entirely letters, newspaper dispatches, official reports, a treaty text and, for the nations, speeches taken down in English by the other side. There are few diaries. The fullest running account was sent from the 'Treaty Ground' to the St. Louis Missouri Republican by its editor, A. B. Chambers, who was also the council's secretary, and by B. Gratz Brown. Every Indigenous speech here reached print through an interpreter, often one named on the treaty, John S. Smith for the Cheyenne or John Pizelle for the Arapaho, and through reporters who called the speeches 'begging'. The book labels them as interpreted and gives them their own lines in the ledger. Set side by side, the records do not agree on what was happening. Mitchell said the Great Father wanted no land; the map that De Smet and Jim Bridger drew on 12 September was presented as taking none, and Article 5 kept every nation's right to hunt and travel across the lines. Yet the Oglala objected at once that the lines cut off their country south of the Platte. The Lakota asked for a chief for each band and were given one head chief, Conquering Bear, chosen by Mitchell. The Shoshone rode five hundred miles to be told they were not parties. Upriver at Fort Union, the Swiss clerk Rudolph Kurz watched the Assiniboine refuse the chief the commissioners had made for them. The nations' own records remember other things. Lakota winter counts name 1851–52 for the great issue of goods on the Platte, or for peace with the Crow, not for roads or boundaries. Hidatsa and Arikara witnesses in 1930, and a Crow elder in 2016, spoke of the treaty as a confirmation of their lands that was later broken. These are set out as positions, with no verdict. The epilogue is administrative. On 24 May 1852 the Senate cut the promised annuities from fifty years to ten, with up to five more at the President's discretion, and made payment depend on the nations' consent. Fitzpatrick and the upper Missouri agent gathered assent in 1853 from every nation except the Crow. On 19 August 1854 Conquering Bear was mortally wounded near Fort Laramie when Lieutenant John Grattan's detachment fired on his camp over an emigrant's cow, and the peace the council had promised on the Platte ended.

intro: In October 1867 some five thousand Gáuigú (Kiowa), Nʉmʉnʉʉ (Comanche), Na'isha (Plains Apache, the record's 'Kiowa-Apache'), Hinono'ei (Arapaho) and Tsitsistas (Cheyenne) people camped along Medicine Lodge Creek in southern Kansas, where it meets Elm Creek, to meet the Indian Peace Commission. The commission had been created by Congress that July to end three years of war on the Plains and to clear the way for railroads and settlement. It came south from Fort Larned with a train of 165 wagons, a cavalry escort, and a press corps. The war had a beginning everyone at the council knew. In November 1864 Colorado volunteers under John Chivington attacked Black Kettle's Cheyenne and Arapaho camp at Sand Creek after its people had been told they were under protection. The commission's own report of January 1868 called it a massacre. At Medicine Lodge a Cheyenne man turned the commissioners' pipe bowl down because his father had died there, and Little Raven named it in his speech. The council produced three treaties. On 21 October the Kiowa and Comanche signed one, and the Plains Apache a second that joined them to it. On 28 October, after the main Cheyenne bands finally came in from the Cimarron, the Cheyenne and Arapaho signed a joint treaty. The nations gave up claims to the country north of the new reservations in the Indian Territory and were promised houses, schools, farming tools, clothing and money for thirty years. They kept a right to hunt south of the Arkansas only while the buffalo lasted. Article 12 of each treaty barred any future cession without the consent of three-fourths of the adult men. Almost none of the record is a diary. The state's side is the commission's journal, kept by its secretary and a shorthand reporter, the treaty texts, and the report to the President. The press is unusually rich: a dozen correspondents, among them a 26-year-old Henry M. Stanley, took the speeches down at tables under the brush arbour. Every Indigenous speech survives only as an interpreter's English taken down by the other side. The interpreters included Philip McCusker for the Comanche, John S. Smith and George Bent for the Cheyenne, and others. Popular modern versions of Satanta's and Ten Bears's speeches are often embellished. This chapter uses only wording from 1867 reports and labels it as interpreted. The Indigenous record also survives in other forms. The Kiowa kept pictographic calendars, and Set-t'an's names this season 'Timber-hill winter' for the wooded hill at the treaty ground, while another Kiowa calendar ignores the treaty altogether. George Bent, the Cheyenne-born interpreter, wrote his memories down forty years later. Two late memoirs, by Bent and by the commissioner's son Alfred Taylor, add camp detail the official papers leave out. They are labelled as late. The epilogue is a court case. In 1903, in Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, the Supreme Court considered the Kiowa claim that the allotment of their reservation without three-fourths consent broke Article 12. It held that Congress could set treaty provisions aside. The promise made aloud to the Cheyenne about hunting north of the Arkansas, which a reporter asked to have written in, belongs to the same story of spoken and written treaties.

intro: In August 1876 the nēhiyawak (Plains Cree), with Nakoda (Assiniboine), Saulteaux and Woods Cree bands, met the Crown's commissioners at Fort Carlton, the old Hudson's Bay post on the North Saskatchewan. Lieutenant Governor Alexander Morris had brought the terms already accepted in Treaties 1 to 5: reserves, a cash present, small annuities, tools and schools. The Cree had asked for a treaty for years, Sweet Grass as early as 1871. They came to it as the buffalo were failing. Between 18 and 23 August the Carlton councils turned on a single question: what would happen to the people while they learned to farm, and if famine came? Pītikwahanapiwīyin (Poundmaker) asked how the offer could feed and clothe his children; Ahtahkakoop asked for food in the planting seasons; Mistawāsis narrowed it to help at the start and in famine. Morris refused daily rations but granted more cattle and implements, three years of seed-time provisions, aid in a general famine or pestilence, and a medicine chest at each agent's house. None of these was in the earlier numbered treaties. Kamīyistowesit (Beardy) signed separately at Duck Lake on 28 August; Wīhkasko-kisēyin (Sweet Grass) signed first at Fort Pitt on 9 September. Mistahi-maskwa (Big Bear) arrived after the signing, would not sign, and asked to be spared the rope about his neck. He held out until hunger brought him to an adhesion at Fort Walsh on 8 December 1882. The record is lopsided, and this chapter says so plainly. Almost everything is the Crown's: Morris's book of 1880, which prints his own report and the day-by-day narrative of his secretary A. G. Jackes, and the treaty text. Every Cree speech here was spoken in Cree, rendered into English by the commission's interpreters or by Peter Erasmus, the Cree-Métis interpreter the chiefs hired themselves, and condensed by Jackes. Quoted lines are labelled 'as interpreted'. Erasmus's memoir, dictated about 1920 and published in 1976, gives the view from inside the chiefs' council, including Poundmaker's line about pemmican that the official record omits. There are no diaries kept on the treaty ground. The nations' own understanding comes down as oral history. Treaty 6 Elders interviewed in 1976 and in the 1990s described a land shared to the depth of a plough, not surrendered, and a medicine chest that meant doctors, medicines and hospitals. The written text records a surrender of land and a chest kept at the agent's direction. These are set side by side here as positions. The courts have also read the clause: Dreaver v. The King (1935) held that medicines must be supplied free; the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal read it narrowly in R. v. Johnston (1966) and R. v. Swimmer (1970); in Wuskwi Sipihk Cree Nation v. Canada (1999) the Federal Court said it may well require a full range of modern medical services. The epilogue runs through the six years Big Bear refused, and through the Saskatchewan Herald, founded at Battleford in 1878, whose editorials called the treaty a contract to farm. Poundmaker and Big Bear were both imprisoned after 1885; Canada exonerated Poundmaker on 23 May 2019. In August 2026, for the 150th anniversary, the manuscript treaty went back inside the walls of Fort Carlton.

intro: On Saturday 15 November 1884 Otto von Bismarck opened a conference of fourteen states in the congress hall of his official residence at Wilhelmstrasse 77 in Berlin. Germany, Britain, France, Portugal, Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain, Italy, Austria-Hungary, Russia, Denmark, Sweden-Norway, the Ottoman Empire and the United States sent delegates. The agenda was African: free trade in the Congo basin, free navigation of the Congo and the Niger, and the formalities for any new occupation of the African coast. No African state or ruler was represented. The General Act was signed on 26 February 1885. The absence is the subject of this chapter. While the delegates sat in Berlin, consuls, naval officers, traders and adventurers were collecting signatures and marks from African rulers. These treaties were the raw material the conference's rules would later process. In the Niger delta the British consul Edward Hyde Hewett carried a printed protection treaty from river to river. In Cameroon two Hamburg firms obtained the sovereignty of the Duala coast, and the German navy attacked the Duala towns that refused it. In the interior opposite Zanzibar, Carl Peters had rulers of Usagara and three neighbouring districts sign German-language contracts with a cross. So the African side of this chapter is not a counter-delegation. It is the rulers who signed, struck out clauses, refused, protested or took up arms during the same months. The record is lopsided, and the chapter says so. The Berlin side survives as printed protocols in French (published in English in the British Parliamentary Papers and in US government documents), diplomatic dispatches, a newspaper or two, and the Act itself. The African side survives mostly as treaties drafted by Europeans, letters and protests preserved in European archives or reported by European officials, and a few printed reactions from the West African press. Many of the rulers' words reach us only through consuls' paraphrases or translations. Those entries are labelled so, and none of them is presented as a ruler's own wording. There are almost no diaries here. The forms are speeches recorded in minutes, dispatches, letters, treaty texts, a naval officer's diary published thirty years later, and editorials. The delegates' stated aims are reported as they stated them. Britain's instructions asked that the welfare of the natives not be neglected. Article 6 of the Act bound the powers to watch over the native tribes and suppress the slave trade. The US delegate spoke of the consent of native peoples. The African responses are also reported as their authors made them: Jaja of Opobo crossing out a free-trade article, Nana Olomu reserving two articles, Kum'a Mbape (called Lock Priso by the British and Germans) telling the Germans to take their flag down, Sultan Barghash of Zanzibar protesting that the lands Peters had 'acquired' were his, and the Lagos Observer in February 1885 calling the whole proceeding a robbery. The chapter offers no verdict on these positions. It sets them side by side by date. The chapter begins in July 1884, the summer of signatures that produced the claims argued over in Berlin. It runs through the conference and ends in August 1885, when German warships off Zanzibar obtained the Sultan's acknowledgement of the protectorate that the Kaiser had granted on 27 February, the day after the Act was signed. Two later dates on Jaja's side (1887) are included because they show how his reading of the 1884 promise played out.

intro: In 1888 the kingdom of the amaNdebele (Ndebele, called 'Matabele' in the English record), ruled from Bulawayo by Lobengula Khumalo, became the target of a crowd of concession-seekers. Gold had been found on the Witwatersrand in 1886, and men in Kimberley and London believed the high country to the north, which the amaNdebele raided and claimed, might hold a second Rand. In February 1888 the missionary-turned-official John Smith Moffat obtained the king's mark on a short treaty of friendship. Under it Lobengula undertook not to deal with any foreign power over his territory without the British High Commissioner's sanction. Eight months later, on 30 October 1888, Charles Rudd, Rochfort Maguire and Francis 'Matabele' Thompson, acting for Cecil Rhodes, obtained his mark on a single page granting them 'complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals' in his kingdoms. In return they promised £100 every lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles with 100,000 rounds, and a steamboat on the Zambezi or £500 in its place. This chapter sets the documents of that one negotiation side by side. They are: the concession text and the missionary Charles Helm's certificate that he had explained it; Rudd's journal of the journey; Thompson's later autobiography; the letters and public notices Lobengula dictated to white scribes at Bulawayo; the reported words of his two senior izinduna (councillors), Mshete and Babayane, who went to Windsor in March 1889; the letter written in Queen Victoria's name in reply; the questions put in the House of Commons; and later recollections from people who were at Bulawayo in 1889. The record is mostly letters, notices, parliamentary answers and memoirs written long afterwards rather than diaries, and the form tags say so. Almost nothing survives in the amaNdebele's own hand. Lobengula's letters were written in English by missionaries, traders or rival concession-seekers, each with an interest of his own, and his councillors' words reached London through interpreters. The central dispute is the gap between the page and the conversation. The written text grants minerals, the power to do what was needed to win them, and the right to exclude rival concession-seekers. It sets no limit on how many men might come. Helm later confirmed that Rudd had also made spoken promises that never went into the document: that no more than ten white men would come to dig, that they would not dig near towns, and that they would obey the laws of the country. Lobengula's letters of 1889 say he had been told one thing and had signed another. The grantees and their supporters held that the king and his council had had the paper explained and had accepted its terms with the rifles in view. The chapter sets these positions out without a verdict. The concession became the legal foundation of the British South Africa Company, whose royal charter was granted on 29 October 1889. On the way there it produced a public repudiation, a diplomatic mission to the Queen, a Commons debate about arms and monopoly, and a political crisis at Bulawayo. In that crisis the king's senior councillor Lotshe Hlabangana, who had advised accepting the rifles, was put to death with members of his household in September 1889. The epilogue is brief. In 1890 the Company's Pioneer Column occupied Mashonaland. In 1893 the Company made war on the amaNdebele kingdom. Bulawayo was burned and abandoned in November, and Lobengula died in the north in January 1894. The vantage points run from the king's own enclosure, through the missionary-interpreter who stood between the parties, out to Kimberley, Cape Town, Westminster and Windsor, and on to the 1930s, when an amaNdebele veteran told his story to a British scholar. Read together, they show how few hands the words passed through, and how much depended on who was holding the pen.
